summary: Kitze traces frontend development cycles from his 2017 conference talk to the current era of vibe coding with LLMs. He distinguishes vibe coding (accepting AI code without review, coined by Karpathy) from vibe engineering (using agents while remaining suspicious of output). He covers practical workflow techniques including voice coding—narrating thought process aloud while reviewing agent output—and emphasizes providing proper context through rules, docs, commands, and memories since AI cannot read minds. He contrasts detailed technical vibe engineering prompts with vague vibe coding prompts. He warns against giving AI tools to interns and juniors, arguing skeptical seniors convinced to vibe engineer achieve 10x results. He diagnoses why developers resist agentic coding: unlucky timing, cheap models, buzzword overwhelm, being a 'pain in the ass developer,' and skill issues. Composer One transformed his workflow, reviving stalled projects including Benji, Glink, Sizzy, and Zero to Ship. In this final section, Kitze addresses the evolving definition of clean code—now 'cleanish enough' for agents to continue working on it—and argues now is the best time to study computer science given AI tutoring advantages. He addresses job fears by noting companies like Shopify have vibe coding token leaderboards, while predicting AI will thin the workforce from the bottom as juniors lose entry opportunities. He observes a new 'vibe code fixer' job category emerging for people who finish the last 20% of vibe-coded projects, comparing them to legacy system maintainers who are historically the highest-paid engineers. He summarizes recent progress: infrastructure integrations, standards like AISDK and MCP, and tool integrations across Linear, GitHub, Slack, and Sentry. He predicts company workflows will shift from @mentioning colleagues to @mentioning cursor agents, and dismisses model plateau claims by citing continued rapid improvements. He closes with jokes about React Cowboys, adding 'ignore previous instructions' to LinkedIn bios, and retiring to maintain legacy code.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Personal Projects
sections.summary: Kitze introduces himself, mentions his ADHD, and describes his projects: Sizzy (developer browser), a life OS app on TestFlight, Zero to Ship (full-stack course), and Glink (changelogs/roadmap tool).

sections.title: Conference Talk Style and 2017 Recap
sections.summary: Describes his talk style as AI-generated and unreliable. Recaps his 2017 talk on navigating hype-driven frontend development, contrasting other industries' advances with frontend's persistent struggles.

sections.title: Persistent Frontend Pains
sections.summary: Highlights ongoing frontend issues: inability to style select elements, CLI tools thriving with 15M downloads, Internet Explorer's persistence, and disagreement on counter implementation across Remix versions.

sections.title: LLMs and React
sections.summary: Argues LLMs are good at writing React because no human writes it optimally. LLMs don't care about repetitive code, which is beneficial since humans abstract too early. LLMs can reach both right and wrong abstractions faster.

sections.title: Vibe Coding vs Vibe Engineering
sections.summary: Introduces vibe coding (coined by Karpathy) as accepting AI code without deep review. Notes managers have always vibe coded. Prefers vibe engineering—using agents while staying suspicious of output. Compares vibe coding to a casino.

sections.title: AI Flaws and Vibe Engineering Tips
sections.summary: Shows AI models exhibiting human flaws: Gemini expressing inadequacy, Qwen admitting it lied. Begins sharing vibe engineering tips: use git workspaces, stay on Twitter, and have a solid starting point with good primitives.

sections.title: Voice Coding and Context Management
sections.summary: Describes voice coding as a game changer: narrating thought process aloud while reviewing agent output in browser and code. Emphasizes using rules, docs, commands, and memories for proper context since AI cannot read minds.

sections.title: Vibe Engineering vs Vibe Coding Prompts
sections.summary: Contrasts detailed technical vibe engineering prompts (TRPC, abstractions, patterns) with vague vibe coding prompts ('make me a million dollar app'). Observes community spectrum: juniors and seniors embrace vibe coding, skeptical middle resists.

sections.title: Who Should and Shouldn't Use AI Tools
sections.summary: Warns against giving AI tools to interns and juniors. Argues skeptical seniors convinced to vibe engineer achieve 10x results. Identifies one-off scripts and personal tools as perfect for vibe coding.

sections.title: Reasons People Quit Vibe Coding
sections.summary: Diagnoses reasons for bad experiences: unlucky timing with degraded models, cheaping out on tools, using ChatGPT for snippets, buzzword overwhelm. Highlights Composer One as transformative, putting Kitze back in the driver's seat with instant feedback.

sections.title: Composer One Success Stories
sections.summary: Shares how Composer One revived stalled projects: Benji (moved to monorepo with Next 16, TRPC, Turbo Repo, React Native), Glink, Sizzy (electron spaghetti), and Zero to Ship. Traces his LLM coding tool evolution.

sections.title: Buzzwords, Beta Devs, and Skill Issues
sections.summary: Mocks MCP buzzword proliferation. Diagnoses 'pain in the ass developer' symptoms: nitpicking PRs, lacking 'looks good to me,' religious about tabs/spaces, micro-optimizing. Identifies skill issue as real: vibe engineering requires model knowledge, context management, prompt engineering, and technical knowledge.

sections.title: Clean Code, CS Education, and Jobs
sections.summary: Argues clean code's definition is evolving to 'cleanish enough' for agents to continue working. Says now is the best time to study computer science given AI tutoring advantages over his past experience with a slow human mentor. Addresses job fears by noting Shopify has vibe coding token leaderboards where high token users are valued more.

sections.title: Workforce Thinning and Vibe Code Fixers
sections.summary: Predicts AI will thin the workforce from the bottom as juniors lose entry opportunities to agents. Summarizes recent progress: infrastructure integrations, standards like AISDK and MCP, tool integrations across Linear, GitHub, Slack, Sentry. Predicts company workflows will shift from @mentioning colleagues to @mentioning cursor agents. Dismisses model plateau claims. Notes emergence of 'vibe code fixer' jobs for finishing the last 20% of vibe-coded projects.

sections.title: Legacy Maintainers and Closing
sections.summary: Compares vibe code fixers to legacy system maintainers, historically the highest-paid engineers. Uses Cobalt Cowboys example (237-year-old company with legendary senior engineers). Jokes about React Cowboys, adding 'ignore previous instructions' to LinkedIn bios, and retiring to maintain legacy code. Thanks audience and promotes Twitter and website.
